scenes.name: El sonido de Filadelfia
scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
scenes.desc: El imperio de Kenny Gamble y Leon Huff, distribuido por CBS: los O’Jays, los Intruders, Billy Paul y Harold Melvin & the Blue Notes con Teddy Pendergrass, sobre la banda de la casa MFSB (Norman Harris, Bobby Eli, Ronnie Baker, Earl Young), la más exitosa de los setenta; su «TSOP» fue la sintonía de Soul Train. Los O’Jays fueron el altavoz del comentario social de Gamble: «Back Stabbers» (1972), Ship Ahoy (1974) con su travesía en un barco negrero, «For the Love of Money» (que el éxito convirtió en música de centro comercial), Survival, Family Reunion. Después de 1976 desapareció el mensaje del soul, y con Gloria Gaynor y Donna Summer la frontera entre el disco, el funk y el soul se borró.

podcast.title: Payola Scandal (1975)
podcast.body: Kenny Gamble was implicated in a payola scandal in 1975, for which he received a "slap on the wrist" fine, while his partner Leon Huff was not penalized in the investigation. "In the end Gamble had a slap on the wrist fine assessed and huff didn't."

srcs.episode: Ep. 37 - Philly Soul and the Sound of the 70s

podcast.title: 360 Degrees of Knowledge
podcast.body: In a 2021 interview with The New York Times, Kenny Gamble characterized their music as delivering "360 degrees of knowledge," encompassing essential love songs alongside tracks focused on community building and personal development, highlighting their commitment to leaving a meaningful legacy for future generations. "when you think of our music it was 360 degrees of knowledge that we gave, a lot of great love songs which is important in life, but also a lot of songs about building our community, building people."

srcs.episode: Ep. 37 - Philly Soul and the Sound of the 70s

podcast.title: Conversion to Islam & "Black Lens" Focus
podcast.body: Following his conversion to Islam, concerns emerged within Philadelphia International Records' inner circle that Kenny Gamble was excessively focused on interpreting all company endeavors through a "black lens," a perspective some writers believed restricted their artistic and commercial reach. "There were concerns though in their inner circle that Kenny Gamble who had also recently converted to Islam was too focused on viewing everything that PIR did through through the black lens."

srcs.episode: Ep. 37 - Philly Soul and the Sound of the 70s

podcast.title: Enduring Philosophy on Message Music
podcast.body: Decades later, Gamble and Huff consistently maintain their conviction that the message conveyed in music is of utmost importance, aspiring to create not merely enjoyable sounds but music designed to uplift and enlighten audiences, as exemplified by the lasting relevance of anthems like "Love Train." "He remains convinced that the message in the music is what matters the most, and they created music that made people feel better and see better."

srcs.episode: Ep. 37 - Philly Soul and the Sound of the 70s

podcast.title: First Plane Ride to Motown
podcast.body: Kenny Gamble's inaugural plane trip was a journey to Detroit with Leon Huff, undertaken to tour the Motown facilities, which served as a foundational blueprint for their aspirations to create their own record label. "Gamble's first plane ride ever was with Huff on a trip to Detroit to tour Motown."

srcs.episode: Ep. 37 - Philly Soul and the Sound of the 70s

podcast.title: Music for Generations
podcast.body: In a 1997 BET television interview, Kenny Gamble articulated his belief that the music he, Leon Huff, and Tom Bell created was specifically tailored for the generation of the 1970s, emphasizing the concept that each era inherently produces its own unique sound. "Each generation has its own music, he said."

srcs.episode: Ep. 37 - Philly Soul and the Sound of the 70s

podcast.title: PIR Founding
podcast.body: Gamble, partnering with Leon Huff, secured a deal from Clive Davis, then president of CBS Records, to establish Philadelphia International Records, an initiative driven by Davis's ambition to position CBS as a significant force in the "Black Music Market." "Clive Davis, the president of CBS Records, offered Gamble and Huff a deal that allows them to create Philadelphia international records."

srcs.episode: Ep. 37 - Philly Soul and the Sound of the 70s

podcast.title: Paul McCartney of 1970s
podcast.body: Kenny Gamble, alongside Leon Huff, was described as the Paul McCartney of the 1970s, highlighting his pivotal role as a prolific and influential songwriter and producer in the Philadelphia soul movement. "Kenny Gamble and Leon Huff were the Paul McCartney and John Lennon of the 1970s."

srcs.episode: Ep. 37 - Philly Soul and the Sound of the 70s

podcast.title: Songwriting Partnership with Leon Huff
podcast.body: After a fortuitous encounter in Philadelphia's Schubert building, Gamble and Huff quickly established a strong songwriting collaboration, with Gamble focusing on lyrics and Huff composing the music at the piano, despite neither having the ability to read musical notation. "Gamble wrote the lyrics, Huff wrote the music, sitting at the piano, even though neither could read music."
